claims.text: The test material is an equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy, corresponding to approximately 20 at.% of each element.
Homogenization and annealing will produce a random solid-solution microstructure in WTaTiVZr.
The random atomic arrangement in WTaTiVZr creates significant local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions in WTaTiVZr lower the energy or Peierls barrier for edge-dislocation motion.
Under high-temperature loading, deformation in WTaTiVZr is dominated by mobile edge dislocations.
Plastic flow in pure tungsten is primarily controlled by screw dislocations.
Relative to pure tungsten, high-temperature loading favors edge-dislocation activation and mobility in WTaTiVZr.
Easier edge-dislocation nucleation and glide allow WTaTiVZr to accommodate more plastic strain and dissipate more energy.
Edge-dislocation-mediated deformation delays crack initiation and propagation in WTaTiVZr.
WTaTiVZr will have a higher strain-to-failure than commercially pure tungsten under matched high-temperature loading.
WTaTiVZr will absorb more mechanical energy before failure than commercially pure tungsten under matched high-temperature loading.
Deformed WTaTiVZr will exhibit a higher density and mobility of edge dislocations than deformed pure tungsten.
Commercially pure tungsten has limited plasticity and lower toughness under comparable high-temperature conditions.
Temperatures of 1200–1600 °C are relevant to sustained plasma-facing-component mechanical service.
Prior work attributes the high strength and high-temperature strength retention of NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV refractory HEAs to edge dislocations.
BCC elemental metals and dilute alloys are generally controlled by screw dislocations during plastic flow.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to other compositions, processing histories, or conditions outside the high-temperature regime.
